## Overview

Welcome to **BioEngineeR 2026**! The next steps will guide you through the software installation and self-paced learning required before the workshop. Please complete these prerequisites before the workshop begins.

::: callout-note
## Estimated Time

**3-4 hours** (including installation and self-paced learning)
:::


## 1. Software Installation

### 1.1 Install R

R is a free, open-source programming language for statistical computing and graphics.

::: panel-tabset
#### Windows

1.  Visit [CRAN R Project](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/)
2.  Click **"Download R-4.x.x for Windows"** (latest version)
3.  Run the downloaded `.exe` file
4.  Follow the installation wizard (accept all defaults)
5.  Click **Finish** when complete
6.  Optional Step (Recommended): Install RTools (http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/)

#### macOS

1.  Visit [CRAN R Project for macOS](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/)
2.  Download the appropriate version:
    -   **Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)**: `R-4.x.x-arm64.pkg`
    -   **Intel Mac**: `R-4.x.x-x86_64.pkg`
3.  Open the downloaded `.pkg` file
4.  Follow the installation prompts
5.  Move R to your Applications folder
6.  Optional Step (Recommended): Install RTools (https://mac.r-project.org/tools/)
:::

### 1.2 Install RStudio

RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) that makes working with R much easier.

1.  Visit [Posit Downloads](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)
2.  Scroll to **"RStudio Desktop"** section
3.  Choose Operating System
4.  Click **"Download RStudio"**
5.  Run the downloaded `.exe`/`.dmg` file
6.  Follow installation wizard (Windows)/ Drag RStudio to your Applications folder (Mac)

### 1.3 Verify Installation

1.  Open **RStudio** (not R)
2.  In the Console pane (bottom-left), type:

``` r
R.version.string
```

3.  You should see output like: `"R version 4.5.x (202x-xx-xx)"`

::: callout-tip

## 2. RStudio Interface Overview

RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) designed to help you be more productive in your daily data science work.

After you have installed [R](https://cloud.r-project.org/) and [RStudio](https://posit.co/downloads/), you are ready to begin this section!

When you start RStudio, you’ll see four key regions or “panes” in the interface: the Source pane, the Console pane, the Environment pane and the Output Pane.

### **RStudio Panes**

1.  The **Source pane** is where you can edit and save R or Python scripts or author computational documents like Quarto and R Markdown.

2.  The **Console pane** is used to write short interactive R commands.

3.  The **Environment pane** displays temporary R objects as created during that R session.

4.  The **Output pane** displays the plots, tables, or HTML outputs of executed code along with files saved to disk.

![A screenshot of the RStudio UI. There are 4 primary panes, the source, console, environment, and output panes.](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/get-started/images/rstudio-panes-labeled.jpeg){alt="A screenshot of the RStudio UI. There are 4 primary panes, the source, console, environment, and output panes."}

### **Blank slate**

When you quit R, do not save the workspace to an .Rdata file. When you launch, do not reload the workspace from an `.Rdata` file. Long-term reproducibility is enhanced when you turn this feature off and clear R’s memory at every restart. Starting with a blank slate provides timely feedback that encourages the development of scripts that are complete and self-contained.

In RStudio, set this via **Tools** \> **Global Options**, making sure to clear “Restore .RData into Workspace at Startup” and choosing **Never** on the “Save workspace to .RData on exit”.

![A screenshot of Tools \> Global Options in RStudio. It highlights turning off the saving of workspace and restoration of .RData into workspace.](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/get-started/images/blank-slate.png){alt="A screenshot of Tools > Global Options in RStudio. It highlights turning off the saving of workspace and restoration of .RData into workspace."}

### **RStudio Projects**

RStudio projects make it straightforward to divide your work into multiple contexts, each with their own working directory, workspace, history, and source documents.

To create a new project in the RStudio, use the **File** \> **New Project** command.

In the **New Project** wizard that pops up, select **New Directory**, then **New Project**. Name the project “hello-ggplot2” and then click the **Create Project** button.

This will launch you into a new RStudio Project inside a new folder called “hello-ggplot2”.

RStudio projects give you a solid workflow that will serve you well in the future:

-   Create an RStudio project for each data analysis project.

-   Keep data files there; we’ll talk about loading them into R in [Local Data](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/data/data-local.html).

-   Keep scripts there; edit them, run them in bits or as a whole.

-   Save your outputs (plots and cleaned data) there.

Everything you need is in one place, and cleanly separated from all the other projects that you are working on.

Before the workshop, familiarize yourself with RStudio's four main panes:

| Pane | Location | Purpose |
|------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Source** | Top-left | Write and edit R scripts |
| **Console** | Bottom-left | Run R commands interactively |
| **Environment** | Top-right | View loaded data and objects |
| **Files/Plots/Help** | Bottom-right | Navigate files, view plots, access documentation |

### Recommended Video (10 min)

Watch this brief orientation: [A Quick Tour of RStudio](https://youtu.be/SdMPh5uphO0?si=vSmE90bitFBVaIn_) by Posit (formerly RStudio)


## 3. R Programming Basics

Complete the following self-paced learning (~2 hours) to build foundational skills.

### Core Concepts to Learn

Before the workshop, ensure you understand:

- [ ] How to create and run an R script
- [ ] Basic data types (numeric, character, logical)
- [ ] Vectors and data frames
- [ ] Installing and loading packages
- [ ] Using the pipe operator (`|>` or `%>%`)

*Step 1: Programming Basics*
Practice R directly in your browser — no installation needed:
https://r-primers.andrewheiss.com/basics/02-programming-basics/

*Step 2: Workflow Basics*
Read this chapter from R for Data Science (2e):
<https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-basics.html>
